---
applyTo: "app/policies/**/*.rb,app/controllers/**/*.rb,app/views/**,app/forms/**/*.rb"
---

# Pundit

- You MUST NOT add `verify_authorized` or `verify_policy_scoped` to individual controllers. The `PunditAuthorization` concern in `ApplicationController` already adds them.
- Leave `new?` and `edit?` out of a policy unless they differ from `create?` and `update?`. `ApplicationPolicy` calls `create?` from `new?` and `update?` from `edit?`, and forbids every other permission by default.
- In a permission, read the user's roles and the record, with a role on the record last, e.g. `user.app_admin? || record.user_is_copy_editor?(user) || record.user_is_author?(user) || record.user_is_coauthor?(user)` in `PostPolicy#update?`.
- Check a role on the record with the model's `user_is_<role>?` method, e.g. `record.user_is_author?(user)`, and filter a scope with its `for_user_as_<role>` scope, e.g. `scope.for_user_as_author(user)`. Write the role's condition in the model, not in the policy. Check a role on the whole app on the user when it covers every record, e.g. `user.app_admin?`. When it only covers some records, check it through the model, e.g. `record.user_is_copy_editor?(user)`.
- You SHOULD NOT run a `where` query in a permission a view checks for every record in a list, e.g. `user.coauthorships.where(post_id: record.id).exists?` in `PostPolicy#show?`. Read loaded values instead, e.g. `record.user_is_coauthor?(user)` on a preloaded association.
- When such a permission checks whether a record has any associated records, e.g. `record.comments.any?`, you SHOULD add a counter cache to the association, e.g. `belongs_to :post, counter_cache: true` on `Comment` with a `comments_count` column on `posts`. Call `any?` without a block, so it reads the count.
- You SHOULD NOT add conditions beyond what they need to a permission a view checks for every record in a list, e.g. `show?` for each post's link in `app/views/posts/index.html.erb`. A list loaded through `policy_scope` only holds records the user can see.
- Only check for a missing user in a permission for an action a Guest can reach, e.g. one that skips `authenticate_user!`. Check with a guard clause before the role checks, e.g. `return false unless user` in `PostPolicy#show?`, after `return true if record.published?`. Other permissions can assume a signed-in user.
- Put the permission for a nested resource's action in the parent's policy when the check needs the parent. Name it after the task, under the heading for its feature or association, e.g. `PostPolicy#publish?` under `### Publishing ###` and `PostPolicy#create_comment?` under `### Comments ###`. You MUST NOT write a policy for the nested resource for these checks, e.g. `Posts::PublicationPolicy`. Call it with the parent and the permission, e.g. `authorize @post, :publish?` in `Posts::PublicationsController#create`. A check on the nested record itself stays in its own policy, e.g. `authorize @comment` uses `CommentPolicy#destroy?`.
- Lay out each policy in this order: the `Scope` class, then a permission for each controller action in controller order (`index?`, `show?`, `new?`, `edit?`, `create?`, `update?`, `destroy?`, then custom actions in alphabetical order), then other permission checks under comment headings named after the association or feature they cover, in alphabetical order, e.g. `### Comments ###` with `create_comment?` and `approve_comments?`, and `### Publishing ###` with `update_published?`, named after the model's `concerning :Publishing` block, then `### Permitted Attributes ###` last, with only the permitted attributes methods, e.g. `permitted_attributes`. You MUST NOT put another heading after `### Permitted Attributes ###`. Leave out any permission or heading the policy does not need. Put private methods last, after `private`.
- Each policy's `Scope#resolve` SHOULD list exactly the records `show?` allows, with the same checks in the same order, e.g. `return scope.published unless user`, then `return scope.all if user.app_admin? || user.publishing_manager?` in `PostPolicy::Scope#resolve`. An app MAY leave records out of its lists that `show?` still allows, e.g. archived posts. Follow the app's existing scopes. Use the same scope for every list of the model.
- In `resolve`, return a relation, e.g. `scope.published.or(scope.for_user_as_author(user))`. You MUST NOT filter the records in Ruby, e.g. `scope.select { |post| post.published? }`.
- In controllers, load every list through `policy_scope`, after `authorize`, and preload the associations its permission checks read, e.g. `@posts = policy_scope(Post).includes(:coauthorships)` in `PostsController#index` and `@comments = policy_scope(@post.comments)` in `Posts::CommentsController#index`. When an `index` action lists no records, call `skip_policy_scope` after `authorize`. You MUST NOT use `skip_after_action :verify_policy_scoped`.
- Load a single record with `find`, then `authorize` it, e.g. `@post = Post.find(params[:id])`. An app MAY load single records through the scope instead, e.g. `@post = policy_scope(Post).find(params[:id])`, so a record the user can't see returns 404 Not Found. Follow the way the app's existing controllers load records.
- Call `authorize` on the first line of every action. Pass the record when the action has one, and the class when it does not, e.g. `authorize @post` in `show` and `update`, and `authorize Post` in `index`, `new` and `create`.
- When an action needs no authorisation check, call `skip_authorization` on its first line, e.g. `def about; skip_authorization; end` in `PagesController`. You MUST NOT use `skip_after_action :verify_authorized`.
- In a nested resource's `BaseController`, check the parent with `pundit.authorize`, which does not mark the request as authorised, e.g. `pundit.authorize(@post, query: :show?, policy_class: PostPolicy)` in `Posts::BaseController#set_post`. You MUST NOT use plain `authorize` there. Each nested action still calls `authorize` itself, e.g. `authorize Comment` in `Posts::CommentsController#index`. `pundit.authorize` needs Pundit 2.4 or later.
- In a nested resource's `BaseController`, override `handle_not_authorized_error` from the `PunditAuthorization` concern. Redirect to the parent record when it is set and the user can see it, and call `super` otherwise, e.g. `if @post && policy(@post).show?` then `redirect_to @post, alert: "You are not authorized to perform this action."`, else `super`, in `Posts::BaseController`.
- Optionally, when the user cannot see the parent record but can see its index, redirect to the index before falling back to `super`, e.g. `elsif policy(Post).index?` then `redirect_to posts_url, alert: "You are not authorized to perform this action."` in `Posts::BaseController#handle_not_authorized_error`.
- Put permitted attributes in the policy, not the controller. Define `permitted_attributes` and return an explicit list, e.g. `PostPolicy#permitted_attributes` returns `[:title, :body]`. You MUST NOT return every column, e.g. `Post.column_names`.
- In controllers, keep a private params method named after the resource that calls Pundit, e.g. `post_params` returns `permitted_attributes(@post)`. Actions use it as usual, e.g. `@post.update(post_params)`.
- Only fall back to the class when `@post` can be nil while `post_params` runs, e.g. `permitted_attributes(@post || Post)` when `create` calls `Post.new(post_params)`. If every action that calls `post_params` has already set `@post`, pass `@post` alone.
- When actions accept different attributes, replace `permitted_attributes` with one method per action, e.g. `permitted_attributes_for_create` and `permitted_attributes_for_update`. You MUST NOT keep a plain `permitted_attributes` next to them. Keep a single `post_params` in the controller.
- Write each action's list in full, even if attributes repeat, e.g. `permitted_attributes_for_create` returns `[:title, :body, :slug]` and `permitted_attributes_for_update` returns `[:title, :body]`. You MUST NOT build one list from another.
- When only some users can change an attribute, add a permission method named `update_<attribute>?` to the policy, e.g. `PostPolicy#update_published?` returns `user.app_admin? || user.publishing_manager?`. In the permitted attributes method, start with the attributes every user can set, then append the restricted attribute when its check is true, e.g. `attributes << :published if update_published?`.
- Use the policy's permitted attributes only for the main app. In controllers for other APIs, e.g. `Api::V1::PostsController`, define `post_params` with `params.require` and `permit` instead. Reuse the policy's `update_<attribute>?` checks for restricted attributes, e.g. `attributes << :published if policy(@post).update_published?`.
- You MUST NOT build a policy for a record in a view, e.g. `policy(@post).update?` or `policy(post).update?` in `app/views/posts/index.html.erb`. Only call `policy` in a view with a class or a symbol, e.g. `policy(Post).new?` or `policy(:admin).index?`.
- When the app uses Draper, check a record's permissions in a view through its decorator, e.g. `post.can_update?` or `post.can_publish?`.
- In forms, use the `policy` and `policy_scope` methods from the `PunditPolicies` concern to limit choices to what the user can pick, e.g. `collection_for_status` adds `"published"` only when `policy(post).update_published?`.
